differences.title: 1. INGEST PATH
differences.leftDesc: QuestDB is built for high-throughput ingestion using columnar storage and batching; it parses and writes in tight loops to minimize per-row overhead. Backpressure is driven by partition/segment boundaries, not per-event locks.
differences.rightDesc: TDengine optimizes ingestion for IoT telemetry with efficient, concurrent write pipelines. It organizes data into time-partitioned structures and reduces contention via internal buffering, letting multiple producers stream without centralized row-level coordination.

differences.title: 2. STORAGE LAYOUT
differences.leftDesc: QuestDB stores series data column-wise with compression-friendly encodings. Time is used to drive partitioning so scans can skip irrelevant segments early, while columnar reads accelerate aggregations across many series efficiently.
differences.rightDesc: TDengine’s on-disk model is optimized around time ranges and tags. It maintains metadata for tags and uses time-based partitions to localize reads and writes, reducing IO during time-bounded queries common in observability and IoT workloads.

differences.title: 3. QUERY EXECUTION
differences.leftDesc: QuestDB’s SQL layer compiles queries into execution plans that favor vectorized operations for filters, projections, and windowed aggregations. This reduces CPU branchiness and increases cache locality during range scans and group-bys.
differences.rightDesc: TDengine focuses its query engine on time-series patterns—range predicates, downsampling, and tag-based selection. Its planner leverages time partitions and tag metadata to avoid scanning irrelevant blocks, improving tail latency for real-time dashboards.

differences.title: 4. TAGS / SCHEMA MODELING
differences.leftDesc: QuestDB models each time series as a table-like structure with columns plus a lightweight symbol/metadata concept (depending on schema). Querying across dimensions leans on fast dictionary encodings for symbols to speed up group-by and filters.
differences.rightDesc: TDengine uses a super table concept where a schema template defines columns and tags are stored as metadata for each child table. Tag-based queries translate into metadata lookups plus partition pruning, keeping ingestion and retrieval aligned.

differences.title: 5. REAL-TIME CONTINUOUS QUERIES
differences.leftDesc: QuestDB is designed for interactive analytics on fresh data: its columnar execution and partition skipping help queries that repeatedly hit “recent time windows.” Window functions operate directly over compact segments without heavy intermediate materialization.
differences.rightDesc: TDengine provides mechanisms for time-based aggregation patterns (often used as rollups/downsampling for dashboards). It stores aggregated results in a way that reduces re-computation across repeated queries for fixed time granularities.

differences.title: 6. INTERNAL DATA SKIPPING
differences.leftDesc: QuestDB relies on time-driven partitioning and compact segment metadata to prune IO during range scans. When predicates narrow the time range or use symbol filters, the engine avoids reading columns/segments that cannot satisfy the query.
differences.rightDesc: TDengine uses both tag metadata and time partitions to decide which data blocks to read. Tag predicates narrow candidate tables first, then time windows prune partitions, minimizing disk reads for multi-device telemetry workloads.

differences.title: 7. OPERABILITY & DEPLOYMENT
differences.leftDesc: QuestDB typically scales through sharding/partitioning strategies that can be operationally straightforward for teams starting with single-node performance. Its developer ergonomics emphasize SQL ingestion/query workflows and predictable resource usage for benchmarks.
differences.rightDesc: TDengine offers operational features geared toward production IoT fleets, including clustering/replication options and management workflows. It aims to keep ingestion stable under sustained streams and provide predictable query behavior across nodes.
